notes:
Oxidation & reduction

  • Classical: oxidation = addition of O$_2$/removal of H$_2$; reduction = removal of O$_2$/addition of H$_2$.
  • Electronic concept: oxidation = loss of electrons (oxidation number increases); reduction = gain of electrons (oxidation number decreases). Oxidising agent gets reduced (gains e$^-$); reducing agent gets oxidised (loses e$^-$).

Oxidation number rules

  • Free element = 0. Simple ion = its charge. H = +1 (except metal hydrides, −1, e.g. NaH). O = −2 (except peroxides −1, e.g. H$_2$O$_2$; OF$_2$, +2). Sum of oxidation numbers in a neutral compound = 0; in an ion = charge on ion.
  • Fluorine is always −1 in compounds (most electronegative element).

Types of redox reactions

TypeDescriptionExample
Combinationelements/compounds combine, one is oxidised/reduced$2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O$
Decompositionone compound breaks into simpler species$2KClO_3\to2KCl+3O_2$
Displacementone element displaces another from a compound$Zn+CuSO_4\to ZnSO_4+Cu$
Disproportionationsame element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced$Cl_2+2OH^-\to Cl^-+ClO^-+H_2O$

Balancing redox equations

  • Oxidation number method: equalise the total increase/decrease in oxidation number.
  • Ion-electron (half-reaction) method: split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions, balance atoms then charge (add H$^+$/OH$^-$ and H$_2$O), then add electrons and combine so electrons cancel. In acidic medium balance O with H$_2$O and H with H$^+$; in basic medium add OH$^-$ to both sides after balancing in acid.

Electrode potential & electrochemical series

  • Standard reduction potential $E^\circ$: more positive = stronger oxidising agent (gets reduced easily); more negative = stronger reducing agent.
  • Order (increasing $E^\circ$, i.e. increasing oxidising power): Li$^+$/Li (most negative, Li strongest reducer) ... F$_2$/F$^-$ (most positive, F$_2$ strongest oxidiser).
  • A species higher (more negative $E^\circ$) can reduce/displace one lower in the series from its salt solution, e.g. Zn displaces Cu$^{2+}$ since $E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn} < E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu}$.

Common oxidising & reducing agents

Oxidising agents: KMnO$_4$, K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$, O$_3$, H$_2$O$_2$ (as oxidiser), conc. HNO$_3$. Reducing agents: H$_2$S, SO$_2$, oxalic acid, FeSO$_4$, H$_2$O$_2$ (as reducer, e.g. with KMnO$_4$). H$_2$O$_2$ is amphoteric (can act as both).

Exam tip

2 questions typically: find oxidation number of an atom in a compound/ion, and identify oxidising/reducing agent or type of redox reaction (often disproportionation). Learn oxidation-number exceptions (peroxides, hydrides, OF$_2$) — these are the most commonly tested trick.

questions.q: The oxidation number of Mn in KMnO$_4$ is
questions.trick: K(+1), O(-2)×4; sum=0 gives Mn = +7 directly.

questions.q: The oxidation number of oxygen in H$_2$O$_2$ is
questions.explanation: In peroxides, oxygen has oxidation number −1 (not the usual −2), since the two O atoms share a single bond and each contributes −1 to balance with 2 H (+1 each).
questions.trick: Peroxide exception: O is $-1$, not $-2$, in H$_2$O$_2$.

questions.q: In the reaction $Zn + CuSO_4 \to ZnSO_4 + Cu$, the substance oxidised is
questions.explanation: Zn (0) loses electrons to become Zn$^{2+}$ (+2): oxidation. Cu$^{2+}$ gains electrons to become Cu (reduction).
questions.trick: Oxidised = loses electrons; the metal going from 0 to a positive ion.

questions.q: The reaction $Cl_2 + 2OH^- \to Cl^- + ClO^- + H_2O$ is an example of
questions.explanation: Chlorine (0) is simultaneously reduced to Cl$^-$ (−1) and oxidised to ClO$^-$ (+1) — the same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction.
questions.trick: Same element split into two oxidation states → disproportionation.

questions.q: The oxidation number of hydrogen in NaH is
questions.explanation: In metal hydrides, hydrogen has oxidation number −1 (Na is +1, sum = 0, so H = −1), an exception to its usual +1.
questions.trick: Metal hydride exception: H is $-1$, not $+1$, in NaH.

questions.q: Which of the following acts as an oxidising agent?
questions.explanation: K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (Cr in +6) readily gets reduced to Cr$^{3+}$ (+3), making it a strong oxidising agent, commonly used in volumetric analysis.
questions.trick: An oxidising agent itself gets reduced — look for the species with a high, reducible oxidation state.

questions.q: The oxidation number of S in Na$_2$S$_2$O$_3$ (sodium thiosulfate) is
questions.explanation: Na$_2$ contributes +2, O$_3$ contributes −6. For a neutral compound: $2 + 2x - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow 2x = 4 \Rightarrow x = +2$ (average oxidation number of the two S atoms).
questions.trick: Sum oxidation numbers to zero for the neutral compound, solve for S (it's an average).

questions.q: A species with more negative standard reduction potential acts as a
questions.explanation: A very negative $E^\circ$ means the species has little tendency to be reduced (gain electrons) and instead readily loses electrons, i.e. it is a strong reducing agent.
questions.trick: More negative $E^\circ$ = weaker pull on electrons = stronger reducing agent.

questions.q: In the electrochemical series, which of the following can displace copper from CuSO$_4$ solution?
questions.explanation: Zn lies above Cu in the electrochemical series (more negative $E^\circ$), so it can reduce Cu$^{2+}$ and displace Cu metal. Ag, Au, Hg lie below Cu and cannot.
questions.trick: Only a metal above Cu (more negative $E^\circ$) in the series can displace it.

questions.q: Balancing $MnO_4^- + Fe^{2+} + H^+ \to Mn^{2+} + Fe^{3+} + H_2O$ by the ion-electron method, the number of electrons transferred per MnO$_4^-$ ion is
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 in MnO$_4^-$ to +2 in Mn$^{2+}$, a gain of 5 electrons per Mn atom.
questions.trick: Electrons transferred = change in oxidation number of the atom being reduced/oxidised.

questions.q: The reaction $2KClO_3 \to 2KCl + 3O_2$ is an example of a
questions.explanation: One compound (KClO$_3$) breaks down into simpler substances (KCl and O$_2$), so this is a decomposition reaction. Within it, Cl goes from +5 to −1 (reduced) while O goes from −2 to 0 (oxidised) — an intramolecular redox change. It is not disproportionation, since that term applies when the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced; here Cl and O are different elements.
questions.trick: One compound → simpler substances = decomposition, even if redox occurs inside.

questions.q: H$_2$O$_2$ is called an amphoteric redox reagent because it can
options: dissolve in both polar and non-polar solvents
act as both an oxidising and a reducing agent
questions.explanation: H$_2$O$_2$ can be reduced to H$_2$O (oxidising agent) or oxidised to O$_2$ (reducing agent), e.g. it reduces acidified KMnO$_4$ but oxidises acidified KI.
questions.trick: H$_2$O$_2$ swings both ways (oxidiser or reducer) → amphoteric redox reagent.

questions.q: The oxidation number of chromium in $Cr_2O_7^{2-}$ is
questions.explanation: O$_7$ = −14; total charge = −2. For 2 Cr: $2x - 14 = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$.
questions.trick: O$_7$ = $-14$, ion charge $-2$; solve $2x-14=-2$ for Cr.

questions.q: In the reaction $2Na + Cl_2 \to 2NaCl$, sodium is
questions.explanation: Na (0) loses one electron to form Na$^+$ (+1): this is oxidation, by definition loss of electrons/increase in oxidation number.
questions.trick: Losing electrons (0 → positive ion) is oxidation, by definition.

questions.q: Fluorine shows an oxidation number of
questions.explanation: Being the most electronegative element, fluorine is always −1 in its compounds; it never shows a positive oxidation state.
questions.trick: Fluorine is the most electronegative element → always $-1$ in compounds, no exceptions.

questions.q: Which of the following is a comproportionation (opposite of disproportionation) type reaction?
options: $Mn^{2+} + MnO_4^- \to MnO_2$ (same element combining from different oxidation states)
questions.explanation: Comproportionation is the reverse of disproportionation: two oxidation states of the same element combine to give one intermediate oxidation state, as Mn(+2) and Mn(+7) both moving toward Mn(+4) in MnO$_2$.
questions.trick: Comproportionation = reverse of disproportionation: two states of one element merge into one.

questions.q: In acidic medium, the ion-electron method balances oxygen atoms by adding
questions.explanation: In acidic medium, excess oxygen on one side is balanced by adding H$_2$O to the other side, and H is then balanced using H$^+$.
questions.trick: Acidic medium: balance O with H$_2$O first, then H with H$^+$.

questions.q: Which pair correctly represents an oxidant and its corresponding reductant in the same reaction $MnO_4^- + 5Fe^{2+} + 8H^+ \to Mn^{2+} + 5Fe^{3+} + 4H_2O$?
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2 (gains electrons, reduced, so MnO$_4^-$ is the oxidising agent); Fe goes from +2 to +3 (loses electron, oxidised, reducing agent).
questions.trick: The species that gets reduced (gains e$^-$) is the oxidant; the one oxidised is the reductant.

questions.q: The oxidation state of nitrogen in NH$_4$NO$_3$ (two different N atoms) are
questions.trick: Compute N separately in each part of the formula (cation and anion) — they need not match.

questions.q: A redox titration between oxalic acid and KMnO$_4$ in acidic medium requires heating because
options: oxalic acid is insoluble in cold water
the reaction is slow at room temperature and needs activation energy
the colour change is visible only when hot
questions.explanation: The oxidation of oxalate ions by MnO$_4^-$ has a high activation energy and proceeds slowly at room temperature, so the solution is usually warmed to about 60°C.
questions.trick: Slow room-temperature kinetics, not solubility, is why this titration needs heating.

questions.q: The oxidation number of oxygen in OF$_2$ is
questions.explanation: Since fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, O takes a positive oxidation number here: F(-1)×2 + O = 0 → O = +2, an exception to the usual -2.
questions.trick: F beats O in electronegativity → O flips to $+2$ in OF$_2$, an exception.

questions.q: The average oxidation number of iron in Fe$_3$O$_4$ (a mixed oxide, FeO·Fe$_2$O$_3$) is
questions.explanation: $3x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 3x = 8 \Rightarrow x = +8/3 \approx +2.67$, the average of one Fe$^{2+}$ and two Fe$^{3+}$ ions.
questions.trick: Mixed oxide = weighted average oxidation state; solve $3x+4(-2)=0$.

questions.q: The oxidation number of sulphur in H$_2$SO$_4$ is
questions.explanation: H$_2$ contributes +2, O$_4$ contributes -8. For a neutral molecule: $2 + x - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6$.
questions.trick: Sum oxidation numbers to zero: H$_2$(+2) + S(x) + O$_4$(-8) = 0 gives S = +6.

questions.q: The oxidation number of Fe in K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] is
questions.explanation: K$_4$ contributes +4, so the complex ion [Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$ has charge -4. CN$^-$ contributes -6, so Fe $= -4-(-6) = +2$.
questions.trick: Balance outside the bracket first (K$_4$ = +4) to find the complex ion's charge, then solve inside.

questions.q: The oxidation number of chromium in CrO$_5$ (chromium peroxide, containing two peroxide linkages) is
questions.explanation: CrO$_5$ has 2 peroxide O–O bonds (4 O atoms at -1 each) and 1 oxide O (-2): $x + 4(-1) + 1(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6$, not +10 as a naive count would suggest.
questions.trick: Count peroxide O's as $-1$ each and the remaining O as $-2$ before solving for Cr.

questions.q: The oxidation number of oxygen in the superoxide ion KO$_2$ is
questions.explanation: K is +1; the O$_2^-$ superoxide ion has a total charge of -1 spread over 2 oxygen atoms, giving each an oxidation number of -1/2.
questions.trick: Superoxide ion O$_2^-$ splits its $-1$ charge over 2 atoms → each O is $-1/2$.

questions.q: The equivalent weight of KMnO$_4$ (M = 158) in acidic medium (n-factor = 5) is
questions.explanation: Equivalent weight $=$ molar mass $/$ n-factor $= 158/5 = 31.6$.
questions.trick: Equivalent weight = molar mass ÷ n-factor — direct division.

questions.q: The equivalent weight of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (M = 294) in acidic medium (n-factor = 6) is
questions.explanation: Equivalent weight $= 294/6 = 49$.
questions.trick: Equivalent weight = molar mass ÷ n-factor — direct division.

questions.q: The volume of 0.1 N KMnO$_4$ required to completely oxidise 100 mL of 0.2 N FeSO$_4$ solution in acidic medium is
questions.explanation: At the equivalence point, $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 \Rightarrow 0.1\times V_1 = 0.2\times100 \Rightarrow V_1 = 200$ mL.
questions.trick: Equivalence point: $N_1V_1=N_2V_2$ — normalities always match at endpoint.

questions.q: By convention, the standard reduction potential of the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is taken as
questions.explanation: The SHE is the reference electrode against which all other standard electrode potentials are measured, arbitrarily assigned $E^\circ = 0$ V.
questions.trick: SHE is the zero reference: $E^\circ = 0$ V by convention, always.

questions.q: Among Li, Na and K, the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution (based on standard electrode potentials) is
questions.explanation: Despite its small size and highest ionisation enthalpy in the gas phase, Li has the most negative standard reduction potential in water due to its very high hydration enthalpy, making it the strongest reducing agent in aqueous solution.
questions.trick: In water, high hydration enthalpy makes Li the strongest reducer despite gas-phase trends.

questions.q: Copper metal cannot displace zinc from ZnSO$_4$ solution because
options: Cu has a smaller atomic radius than Zn
Cu is more reactive than Zn
Cu has a higher (less negative) standard reduction potential than Zn, so it cannot reduce Zn$^{2+}$
questions.explanation: Since $E^\circ_{Cu^{2+}/Cu} > E^\circ_{Zn^{2+}/Zn}$, Cu$^{2+}$ is more easily reduced than Zn$^{2+}$; Cu metal therefore cannot reduce Zn$^{2+}$ ions to displace zinc.
questions.trick: Compare $E^\circ$ values: a metal can't displace one with a more negative $E^\circ$.

questions.q: In the ion-electron method for balancing a redox equation in basic medium, after balancing as if in acidic medium, the H$^+$ ions are eliminated by adding equal moles of
options: OH$^-$ ions to both sides, converting H$^+$ to H$_2$O
questions.explanation: Adding OH$^-$ equal to the number of H$^+$ ions on both sides converts H$^+ + OH^- \to H_2O$, giving the equation appropriate for basic medium.
questions.trick: Basic medium fix: add OH$^-$ to both sides to convert leftover H$^+$ into H$_2$O.

questions.q: The equivalent weight of H$_2$O$_2$ (M = 34) when it acts as an oxidising agent (n-factor = 2) is
questions.explanation: As an oxidiser, O in H$_2$O$_2$ goes from -1 to -2, a gain of 2 electrons per molecule; equivalent weight $= 34/2 = 17$.
questions.trick: As oxidiser, H$_2$O$_2$'s O drops from $-1$ to $-2$ (gains 2e$^-$); eq. wt = M/2.

questions.q: Which of the following represents a disproportionation reaction?
questions.explanation: Cu$^+$ (+1) is simultaneously reduced to Cu (0) and oxidised to Cu$^{2+}$ (+2) — the same element undergoes both oxidation and reduction, the hallmark of disproportionation.
questions.trick: Same species splitting into a lower and higher oxidation state signals disproportionation.

questions.q: In basic medium, MnO$_4^-$ is reduced to MnO$_2$. The number of electrons gained per Mn atom is
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 in MnO$_4^-$ to +4 in MnO$_2$, a gain of 3 electrons (different from the 5-electron change to Mn$^{2+}$ in acidic medium).
questions.trick: Track the oxidation-state drop of Mn to the given product to get electrons gained.

questions.q: When I$^-$ is oxidised to I$_2$, the number of electrons lost per iodide ion is
questions.explanation: I$^-$ ($-1$) loses one electron to become neutral I (0), which then pairs up as I$_2$.
questions.trick: Going from $-1$ to $0$ always means losing exactly one electron.

questions.q: When the equation $2MnO_4^- + \_\_I^- + 4H_2O \to 2MnO_2 + 3I_2 + 8OH^-$ is balanced (basic medium), the coefficient of I$^-$ is
questions.explanation: 2 Mn atoms gain $2\times3=6$ electrons; each I$^-\to\tfrac12$I$_2$ loses 1 electron, so 6 I$^-$ ions are needed to supply 6 electrons, giving 3 I$_2$.
questions.trick: Equate total electrons gained (by Mn) to total electrons lost (by I$^-$) to balance.

questions.q: 20 mL of 0.1 M K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (n-factor = 6) completely oxidises Fe$^{2+}$ (n-factor = 1) in acidic medium. The moles of Fe$^{2+}$ oxidised are
questions.explanation: Equivalents of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7 = 0.1\times6\times0.020 = 0.012$ eq $=$ equivalents of Fe$^{2+}$ $=$ moles of Fe$^{2+}$ (since its n-factor is 1).
questions.trick: Equivalents of oxidant = equivalents of reductant: $N_1V_1$ gives moles via n-factor 1.

questions.q: The reaction $2H_2O_2 \to 2H_2O + O_2$ is an example of a
questions.explanation: Oxygen in H$_2$O$_2$ (-1) is simultaneously reduced to -2 (in H$_2$O) and oxidised to 0 (in O$_2$), so the same element is both oxidised and reduced — disproportionation.
questions.trick: Same O atom split into higher and lower oxidation states → disproportionation again.
